title: Sorting and index decisions
goal: Order records deliberately and control which labels identify rows.
prerequisites: Know filtering, loc, iloc, and table shape.

cells.title: Sort rows by a value
cells.explanation: sort_values() orders whole rows by one or more column values. ascending=False puts larger values first. It returns a new table, so assign the result if you want to keep the order. The index labels travel with their rows and are not automatically renumbered.
cells.code:
df = students()
result = df.sort_values("Score", ascending=False).head(3)
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]])
print("Index labels:", result.index.tolist())

questions.answer: Descending order, from larger scores to smaller scores.

questions.prompt: Who are the top three students by Score?
questions.answer: Fatima with 95, Chloe with 91, and Jamal with 89.

questions.prompt: Why are the printed index labels 5, 2, and 9 instead of 0, 1, and 2?
questions.answer: The original row labels stay attached to the records when the rows are sorted.

cells.task: Find the three lowest scores instead. Keep Student_ID, Name, and Score in result.
cells.hint: Sort ascending and then take head(3).
cells.solution:
df = students()
result = df.sort_values("Score", ascending=True).head(3)[["Student_ID", "Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
cells.solution_note: The three lowest scores are Hassan 58, Dana 65, and Khalid 68. Sorting whole rows keeps each score matched with its student.

check.prompt: Does sort_values rearrange only the selected column's values?
check.feedback: Whole rows move together so their fields stay associated.

cells.watch: head(3) before sorting chooses the first three source rows, not the three highest scores.
cells.takeaway: I can sort a table and identify the top or bottom records.

cells.title: Specify a tie rule
cells.explanation: Rows can tie on a sort column. With one column, kind="stable" preserves their existing order within a tie. To define a new tie rule, sort by several columns and give one ascending flag per column. Clear tie rules make results easier to reproduce and explain.

questions.answer: Chloe, Amira, and Dana all have 80.

questions.prompt: What is their order after this stable sort?
questions.answer: Chloe, Amira, then Dana, preserving their order in the original table.

questions.prompt: Why might a report need a second sort column?
questions.answer: It provides a clear order among equal values, such as alphabetical order among students with the same score.

cells.task: Sort by Score descending, then Name ascending to break ties alphabetically.
cells.solution_note: Bilal remains first with 95. The three scores of 80 are then ordered Amira, Chloe, Dana.

check.prompt: What does a stable sort preserve for equal sort values?
check.feedback: Stability preserves the source order of rows that tie on the sort key.

cells.watch: Alphabetical tie order must be requested explicitly; a stable sort preserves source order instead.
cells.takeaway: I can make the order of tied records explicit.

cells.title: Set, check, and reset an index
cells.explanation: An index labels rows; it is not automatically a unique ID. set_index() chooses the labels, and index.is_unique tells you whether any label repeats. reset_index() moves the current index back into a column and supplies new default row labels. Use reset_index(drop=True) only when you deliberately want to discard the current labels.
cells.code:
df = students()
indexed = df.set_index("Student_ID")
print("Unique index:", indexed.index.is_unique)
result = indexed.reset_index()
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]].head(3))

questions.answer: It is True when no index label repeats. Separate checks are still needed for missing or invalid IDs.

questions.prompt: After reset_index(), is Student_ID a data column again?
questions.answer: Yes. It is restored as a column, while the row index becomes 0 through 11.

questions.prompt: Why could reset_index(drop=True) lose useful information here?
questions.answer: Student_ID is currently the index, so drop=True would discard those IDs instead of restoring them to a column.

cells.task: Set Student_ID as the index, select S003 and S001 in that order, and reset the selected index without losing the IDs.
cells.solution:
df = students()
indexed = df.set_index("Student_ID")
selected = indexed.loc[["S003", "S001"]]
result = selected.reset_index()
print(result[["Student_ID", "Name"]])
cells.solution_note: The selected rows are Chloe and Amira. Their IDs remain in the Student_ID column, and their new row labels are 0 and 1.

check.prompt: Which operation keeps the old index as a column?
check.feedback: reset_index() preserves the old index values in a column unless drop=True is specified.

cells.verify:
assert indexed.index.is_unique and result.equals(df)
assert result.index.tolist() == list(range(12))
cells.watch: Having an index does not guarantee that its labels are unique or non-missing.
cells.takeaway: I can change an index without accidentally discarding record IDs.

cells.title: Reindex to a requested order
cells.explanation: reindex() aligns a table to a specified set of labels and their requested order. Existing labels bring their rows with them; new labels create missing values. This differs from sorting because you supply the desired labels explicitly. Use isna() to inspect newly missing cells.
cells.code:
df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
result = df.reindex(["S003", "S001", "S999"])[["Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Missing name:")
print(result["Name"].isna())

questions.prompt: Where did the S999 row come from?
questions.answer: It was requested in reindex but was absent from the source index, so pandas created a row of missing values.

questions.prompt: Which order will the index have?
questions.answer: S003, S001, S999, matching the order passed to reindex.

questions.prompt: Why is a missing S999 score not automatically a failing score?
questions.answer: There is no source record for S999. Missing data does not establish a measured score or a fail decision.

cells.task: Reindex to S002, S001, and S004, in that order. Confirm that none of their names is missing.
cells.hint: Use only existing IDs and count missing names with .isna().sum().
cells.solution:
df = students().set_index("Student_ID")
result = df.reindex(["S002", "S001", "S004"])[["Name", "Score"]]
print(result)
print("Missing names:", result["Name"].isna().sum())
cells.solution_note: The output is Bilal, Amira, Dana in the requested order, with no missing names. All requested labels exist.

check.prompt: What can reindex do when a requested label does not exist?
options: Raise an error in every case.
Create a row with missing values.
check.feedback: For this unique index, reindex creates missing data for an absent requested label.

cells.verify:
assert result.index.tolist() == ['S003', 'S001', 'S999']
assert pd.isna(result.loc['S999', 'Score']) and result.loc['S003', 'Name'] == 'Chloe'
cells.watch: Reindexing can fail when source labels are duplicated; check uniqueness before using labels as identifiers.
cells.takeaway: I can distinguish sorting existing rows from aligning to a requested index.
